If negative scores mean anti-regulation, -1 is inverted; the evidence points to a mild pro-regulation stance (+1). His 'measured, responsible' framing keeps it from being +2.

score_objections.objection: Every ai_risk source shows him framing AI purely as an economic/national-security race to win faster ('be careful not to go too slow', 'get out of our own way'); the only counterpoint is opposing the state-law moratorium, which is a federalism position, not a safety one. If +1 means 'leans toward taking AI risk seriously', the evidence does not support it; if the scale's positive pole means 'accelerationist', fine. The Ricketts letter (item 6) is an export-control document and should not count toward ai_risk at all.

Sources are mixed rather than one-directional: he co-sponsors BIS reform explicitly to keep chips out of China's hands and signs a letter asking for KYC/security controls on frontier chips (hawkish), while also wanting the diffusion rule's allied caps scrapped and 'other American technologies to flow freely' (looser). A -1 only fits if the scale's negative pole means 'favors selling more chips abroad'; if negative means 'soft on China', the BIS bill and the 'limiting China's ability to develop frontier AI' language argue for 0 or +1.

Punchbowl (items 7 and 10) shows him opposing the Cruz moratorium, i.e. against federal preemption of state AI laws, and E&E (item 3) shows him defending state planning autonomy against FERC. -1 is consistent only if the negative pole means 'opposes preemption'; if negative means 'supports preemption', the sources point the other way.
